doc.title: Herbie Hancock interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, November 18, 1995

title: Synthesizers, MIDI, sequencers and the virtual studio
summary: His lifelong interest in science led to synthesizers; he asked for MIDI and describes sequencers, remote recording and ISDN.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: I’ve got one final question, because I realize we’ve got to let you go because you’ve got to perform tonight. Just talk to us a little bit, feedback, concepts, insights, on your being one of the icons and one of the spearheads of the whole electronic revolution and its ways it either bonds with jazz or dissects jazz or is jazz.

I started playing piano when I was seven. But when I was five I was already building model boats and planes and taking apart things like watches. And I was always curious about how things worked. I’m the same way with people. People fascinate me. I’m always asking them questions and trying to find out what makes them tick. And so I’ve always had this kind of interest in science. As a matter of fact, when I was in college, my first major was electrical engineering, before I switched to music composition. And so when synthesizers came along, it fulfilled something for my life that I never dreamed would be possible, and that is to combine science and music in some kind of way. So I naturally gravitated toward that, because I’ve always been interested in technology. And I’ve always been interested in orchestration too, so a synthesizer to me is a tool for making instruments. It doesn’t have any sound until you program something into it. You know? So it’s like the hammer and the nails, and the wood. You have to have that and then you can make an instrument. And so I can use it as a kind of a orchestration tool. But then since then, there have been other technologies involving computers and sequencing and midi came along. Midi is a way for, I know, this is funny because I was fooling with electronics and music before midi came along. Midi means Musical Instrument Digital Interface. What I noticed is that if I have an album, I think it’s the “Sunlight” album. On the back of this album is all these keyboards, I mean full of keyboards. There’s no way I can get around to all those keyboards. So I remember telling instrument manufacturers, “Why don’t you guys figure out a way to get these instruments to talk to each other” so that — I mean a person only has two hands. I could hear that I’d like this to happen and that to happen, but I can’t get to them all. But if you could figure out an electronic way to get the instruments to talk to each other, then I could play one instrument, and it could actually trigger the sounds on other instruments. So anyway, I guess enough people started talking about that that they took it seriously and they actually formed an alliance which allowed them to make certain standards and make a protocol called Midi. And that led to some other ideas that we never even thought of — that we could start making keyboards that didn’t have keys, just modules, you know. Well they’re not calling them keyboards — sometimes I do — I’ll still call it a keyboard even though © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

it doesn’t have keys, you know? But I’ve got a rack with about, it has other things in it too but it’s got about five or six different like keyboards and modular instruments that can be talked to from another single keyboard. And it gives me the opportunity to, like I said arrange. And also sequencers, which came out of music and computer technology, gave me a chance to — maybe I should explain what that is — a sequencer remembers the notes that I play. And it’s stored in the computer and then it can play back those same codes that contain the notes and play it back through the instrument so that I can listen back to what I played on the very instrument that I played it on. The computer plays it the second time if I put it in a playback mode. And now we can have different tracks. Now they have multi-track recording on the computer. Tapeless recording. Where an instrument gets put into your hard disk. And so this has opened up all kinds of new possibilities for recording in your home. I mean all these parallels are happening also in business, in the business world too, you know. A lot of people are now able to work at home and have computer terminals at home and have them connected through a modem or other device to the office machines, and so it just kind of expands this idea of a virtual office. It’s the same thing like a virtual studio. Now that idea of a virtual studio is really taking shape because now it’s possible, although this technology is very new, to be able to overdub on a recording and not be in the city that’s recording it. It’s remote recording, where you can have a recording session in New York, musicians can lay down certain tracks, and if say they wanted me to overdub a part on that recording on a different track, I can be in Los Angeles, listen to the tracks that have been recorded on, through a high speed telephone linkage, and record from my studio, back through the phone, on to the tape that’s in New York. As a matter of fact I have a set up in my studio now that allows me to do something like that. It just got set up just before I came to — no it’s not even set up yet, it was brought to the studio before I came to New York. You know so I haven’t had a chance to use it there. We did use the same device actually, last night at the Blue Note. Dolby has this device called Dolby Fax Pro and it allows you to send music, high quality sound, down a telephone line. That’s a higher speed line than the regular line, it’s called an ISDN line. But it’s not very expensive, those ISDN lines, and they allow you to really go more than, put more than your toll into the world of, the new world of technology and start getting into the information highway. By the way I should tell you that I’m launching a foundation.
